opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is really the long-term vision behind a lot of our work on what we call hyper-representations. The starting point is a simple observation: we as a community have trained millions of neural networks. They sit on Hugging Face, in model zoos, on people's hard drives. Each of those trained weight sets is basically a data point that encodes what was learned on some task, with some architecture, under some training regime. Yet we mostly treat them as finished artifacts. We download one, fine-tune it, and the rest is forgotten.

So the question we asked was: what if we treat the weights themselves as a data modality? Just like we train foundation models on images or text, could we train a model on populations of neural networks? We started with model zoos, large, systematically generated collections of trained models, and trained self-supervised representation learners on the weight space. What we found is that these representations capture really meaningful properties. From the weights alone you can predict a model's accuracy, its generalization gap, the hyperparameters it was trained with, and so on.

Once you have a learned representation of that space, the natural next step is to make it generative. If you can encode models into a latent space, you can also decode from it and sample new weights. In our experiments, sampled models can serve as better initializations than random init, so they train faster and sometimes reach better performance, and in some cases they work reasonably well right away without much additional training.

The on-demand vision extrapolates from that. Imagine a foundation model that has seen a huge diversity of trained networks across tasks, architectures, and data distributions. Instead of saying "give me a dataset and a GPU budget and I'll train you a model from scratch," you'd condition that generative model on what you need. That could be a description of the task, a few examples of your data, constraints like "it has to run on this microcontroller," or "I need this level of robustness." The model would then generate weights that fit those requirements, or at least a very strong starting point that needs only a little fine-tuning.

There are a few reasons I find this compelling. One is efficiency and sustainability. We burn an enormous amount of compute retraining things that are, in some sense, already known. If knowledge in weight space can be reused and recombined, that's a big win. Another is democratization. Not everybody has the data or the infrastructure to train a good model, but they might be able to describe what they need. A third is more scientific. Learning on weight space tells us something about the structure of the solutions neural networks find, things like symmetries and permutations, and which regions of the space are good.

It's still early, and I want to be honest about that. Scaling to large, heterogeneous architectures is hard. Weight space has nasty symmetries you have to handle, and conditioning generation reliably on tasks is an open problem. But I really see neural networks as data, and a foundation model over that data, as a very natural direction for the field.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the big vision behind the work we've been doing on hyper-representations. The idea is that a trained neural network is itself a data point. If you look at a model zoo, thousands of networks trained on the same task but with different seeds, different hyperparameters, different initializations, you can treat the weights of each of those networks as a sample from some distribution. And then the natural question becomes: can we learn that distribution?

So what we did is we trained an autoencoder on the weights themselves. You flatten the weights, you feed them in, and you learn a compressed latent representation of the model. And what we found, which honestly surprised us at first, is that this latent space is structured. Models with high accuracy cluster together, models trained with certain hyperparameters cluster together. You can actually predict properties of a network, its test accuracy, its generalization gap, even which hyperparameters it was trained with, just from looking at the latent embedding of its weights, without ever running the model on data.

Now, once you have that, the generative direction follows almost immediately. If the latent space is structured and you have a decoder, you can sample from the region of latent space where the good models live, decode, and you get new weights. And those weights work. Not perfectly out of the box, but they're a dramatically better starting point than random initialization. We've shown you can take a sampled model, fine-tune it for a handful of epochs, and reach performance that would otherwise take you a full training run.

So the way I envision it going forward is something like a foundation model, but for models rather than for text or images. You would describe what you want. Maybe you say I need a small classifier for this kind of input distribution, with roughly this capacity, and the system doesn't train from scratch, it generates a candidate from the learned distribution of networks and then adapts it. Think of it as transfer learning, but instead of transferring from one specific pretrained checkpoint, you're transferring from the entire population of models that have ever been trained.

There are of course big open questions. Scaling is the obvious one, we started on small CNNs and we're pushing toward larger architectures. Handling heterogeneous architectures in a single representation is another, because right now most of the structure we exploit comes from the fact that the models share a shape. And there's a deeper question of what the latent space is really encoding, whether it's capturing something like the function the network computes versus just regularities in the parameterization. But I think the direction is very promising. We've gotten used to the idea that we train models by gradient descent on data. The idea that you could instead generate a model, treat training as sampling plus a bit of refinement, is a pretty fundamental shift in how we think about where models come from.

astra-6.text:
The idea is to treat neural networks themselves as the data. Usually, we train a model on text or images. Here, we would train a foundation model on a collection of trained neural networks, learning a representation of their weights and the relationships between them.

Then you could condition that model on a request: this is the task I want to solve, this is the data I have, and these are my computational constraints. Instead of starting a new training run from scratch, you would generate a set of weights that gives you a useful model—or at least a very good initialization that you can adapt with a little additional training.

The difficult part is making that representation meaningful. Two networks can implement the same function while looking quite different in weight space, so simply treating weights as a sequence of numbers isn't enough. And generating weights is only useful if the resulting network actually performs the requested task. You still need to evaluate it.

But that's the opportunity: to reuse the knowledge contained in models we've already trained, and make creating the next model much more efficient.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is to treat neural networks themselves as data. Instead of training a foundation model on text or images, you train it on a population of neural networks—their weights, their architectures, and information about the tasks they solve. You want to learn a representation of that space: what makes networks similar, what makes them different, and how those differences relate to their behavior.

Then you could condition generation on what you need. You might say, “I have this classification task, this much data, and this computational budget. Give me a network that fits those requirements.” The model would generate weights that you could use as an initialization, or potentially as a model that already performs the task.

I think the important distinction is that we’re generating the network itself, rather than just generating code that describes a network and then training it from scratch. You’re trying to reuse the learning already captured in other models.

Of course, that’s the vision. Getting there means dealing with things like the symmetries in weight space: two networks can implement the same function while looking very different in terms of their parameters. And you have to establish that a generated network actually behaves as intended. But if we can solve those problems, it gives us a different way to think about model development—moving from training every model individually toward generating models on demand.
